svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EC2 automatic instance recovery. If AWS detects that an instance is unavailable due to an underlying hardware or software issue, there are two mechanisms that can automatically restore instance availability: simplified automatic recovery and Amazon CloudWatch action based recovery. Simplified automatic recovery is enabled by default during instance launch, has fixed recovery behaviour managed by AWS, excludes metal instance sizes, is not supported for instances that attach instance store volumes at launch, notifies only through the Health Dashboard, and carries no additional cost. CloudWatch action based recovery requires manual configuration of CloudWatch alarms and actions, allows customisable actions and conditions and SNS notification, includes metal sizes, is supported on selected instance types where instance store data is lost during recovery, makes faster recovery attempts than simplified automatic recovery, and might incur CloudWatch charges. Both must be configured in advance on an instance before a system status check fails. The trigger is narrow: if a system status check fails, AWS initiates automatic instance recovery, which attempts to migrate the affected instance to different hardware, and automatic instance recovery does not operate if only the instance status check fails. A failed system status check indicates a problem with the host hardware or software and not a problem with the instance itself, from causes including loss of network connectivity, loss of system power, software issues on the physical host, and hardware issues on the physical host that impact network reachability. The metric to alarm on is StatusCheckFailed_System, where 0 means the system status check passed and 1 means it failed. The trap is that a failed performance status check also increments the aggregate StatusCheckFailed metric, so an alarm wired to the aggregate can enter the ALARM state when a performance status check fails even though the system status check is healthy, which is why AWS documents StatusCheckFailed_System as the metric for recovery actions. Recovery is a migration that presents as an unplanned reboot: AWS attempts to move the instance to a different host and if successful the process will appear to the instance as an unplanned reboot. A recovered instance is identical to the original except for what is lost. Preserved are the instance ID, public, private and Elastic IP addresses, instance metadata, placement group, attached EBS volumes and Availability Zone. Lost are data stored in volatile memory, data on instance store volumes for CloudWatch action based recovery only, and operating system uptime which resets to zero. Notably the instance retains its public IPv4 address during recovery, whereas a manually restarted instance receives a new public IPv4 address unless it has an Elastic IP address. If the recovery process is unsuccessful the instance might continue running on the impaired host and manual intervention is required. Recovery attempts emit Health Dashboard events, AWS_EC2_SIMPLIFIED_AUTO_RECOVERY_SUCCESS or FAILURE for simplified recovery and AWS_EC2_INSTANCE_AUTO_RECOVERY_SUCCESS or FAILURE for CloudWatch action based recovery. These mechanisms are designed for individual instances, and AWS recommends a high-availability architecture for a resilient system.
svg.title: Recovery is a migration that looks like a reboot, and only one check starts it
svg.text: Five status checks exist. Exactly one of them starts a recovery.
“Automatic instance recovery can recover an instance that fails a system status check. However, automatic
instance recovery does not operate if only the instance status check fails.”
Instance store at launch: not supported
The alarm trap, now that a fifth check exists
alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System → recover. 0 = passed, 1 = failed.
NOT on StatusCheckFailed (aggregate) → a degraded GPU also increments this.
An alarm on the aggregate can enter ALARM when a performance check fails and the system check is healthy.
AWS documents StatusCheckFailed_System as the metric for recovery actions.
“AWS will attempt to move your instance from the host with the underlying hardware or software issue to a
different host … will appear to the instance as an unplanned reboot.”
Public, private and Elastic IP addresses
The public IPv4 survives. A stop/start does not keep it.
Anything keyed to uptime restarts its clock.
Both mechanisms “must be configured in advance … before a system status check fails” — there is no retrofit.
Recovery emits Health events per mechanism, so the audit of whether it ever fired is an AWS Health query, not a log search.
And it is per-instance by design: “designed for individual instances”, which is AWS telling you it is not an HA strategy.
